articles.title: Piers Morgan, Katie Zacharia tangle in contentious interview: ‘You sound like a robot’
articles.summary: British broadcaster Piers Morgan clashed with former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia over her abrupt departure from the Trump administration, accusing her of sounding like a “robot” as she repeatedly dodged questions about her five-day tenure. During a contentious interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored” released Wednesday, Morgan pressed Zacharia about her private conversations with…
articles.body:
British broadcaster Piers Morgan clashed with former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia over her abrupt departure from the Trump administration, accusing her of sounding like a “robot” as she repeatedly dodged questions about her five-day tenure .

During a contentious interview on “Piers Morgan Uncensored” released Wednesday, Morgan pressed Zacharia about her private conversations with President Trump before she was ousted earlier this month. Zacharia refused to share details of the exchange, instead repeatedly declaring her loyalty to the president and accusing the media of trying to distract from his agenda.

“Let’s cut the crap here and have a serious genuine conversation,” Morgan said after several unsuccessful attempts to get Zacharia to answer his questions. “You sound like a robot. Has Donald Trump got some program plugged into you to make you come out with all this stuff?”

He continued, “When Donald Trump said to you, ‘Was this really for you?’ what did you say back?”

Morgan was referring to Trump’s public account of Zacharia’s departure; the president said he had asked her about her feelings on the press secretary position following a shaky debut behind the podium and controversy surrounding her legal background .

Zacharia declined to answer, insisting that her conversations with the president would remain confidential.

“Katie, come on!” Morgan responded. “Katie, he’s told the entire world what he said.”

“I’m not going to mince words or split hairs over this,” Zacharia said. “I will not disclose private conversations that I’ve had with the president.”

She pivoted to defending Trump, saying she would continue supporting him regardless of the circumstances surrounding her firing.

“I will continue fighting for him. I am ruthlessly loyal. I have always been, and I will continue to be,” she said.

The exchange grew increasingly heated as Zacharia argued that the interview should be focused on the upcoming midterm elections rather than her brief stint at the White House.

Morgan pushed back, telling her that her departure was precisely why she had been invited on to the show. He also questioned why she was so reluctant to discuss her dismissal when Trump had already spoken publicly about it and did not necessarily show her any loyalty when he fired her after only five days.

Nonetheless, Zacharia did not let up, insisting that she did “not sound like a robot.”

She has previously ripped the media over its coverage of Trump, accusing the press corps of having “ Trump Derangement Syndrome ” while reiterating her loyalty to the president.

articles.title: Nearly 40 House Dems skip effort to end Ilhan Omar immigration probe
articles.summary: Nancy Pelosi and Steny Hoyer were among nearly 40 House Democrats who did not sign Pramila Jayapal's letter defending Ilhan Omar's probe.
articles.body: Nearly 40 House Democrats appear to have shunned an effort by their colleagues to end the federal probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. House Democrats led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., sent a letter to the Trump administration earlier this week demanding a stop to the investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork, arguing it was a bid to sway her re-election campaign ahead of Tuesday's midterm Election Day. The letter was backed by some 175 House Democrats, more than two-thirds of the caucus — though some notable names were left off. Two of three of House Democrats' previous senior leadership did not sign the letter. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer, D-Md., did not sign on. Rep. Nydia Velazquez, D-N.Y., from signing the letter. THE HITCHHIKER'S GUIDE TO WHY REMOVING ILHAN OMAR FROM CONGRESS COULD BE HARDER THAN TRUMP EXPECTS Democrats running in tight races also kept their distance from the public condemnation of the probe. Reps. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, Tom Suozzi, D-N.Y., Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., and Don Davis, D-N.C., are among the names left off the letter as well. articles.title: Most voters say enthusiasm to cast midterm ballots higher than previous elections: Survey
articles.summary: Most American voters say they have a higher level of enthusiasm for casting their ballots this year versus prior elections, according to a new poll. In the Gallup survey, 56 percent of respondents said they were “more enthusiastic about voting than usual,” while 30 percent said they were “less enthusiastic” and 11 percent were “as…
articles.body:
Most American voters say they have a higher level of enthusiasm for casting their ballots this year versus prior elections, according to a new poll.

In the Gallup survey , 56 percent of respondents said they were “more enthusiastic about voting than usual,” while 30 percent said they were “less enthusiastic” and 11 percent were “as enthusiastic” to cast their ballot as they had been before.

The poll comes less than a week out from the midterms, with both chambers of Congress and most governorships up for grabs.

Recent polling has also shown a distaste for Republicans, with Democrats leading them on generic ballots and in multiple key races, including in multiple red or purple states such as Texas and Michigan.

Republicans are facing political headwinds this cycle in the form of slumping approval ratings for President Trump, the unpopular war in Iran and concerns about the cost of living.

Fresh favorable polling for Democrats and the apparent widespread voter enthusiasm in the Gallup poll, if accurate, could spell trouble for the GOP as Election Day inches closer.

The Gallup survey also found that 58 percent of Democrats or respondents leaning Democratic were “more enthusiastic about voting than usual” versus prior elections, compared with 48 percent of Republicans or respondents leaning Republican.

The Gallup poll took place from Oct. 1 to 19, featuring 1,057 registered voters and 4 percentage points as its margin of sampling error.

articles.title: Maine, Kansas Senate races neck and neck as Democrats lead in Texas, Michigan, poll shows
articles.summary: High-profile Senate races in Maine, Texas, Michigan and Kansas are extremely tight, with Democrats leading in all four according to a new CNN poll.
articles.body: High-profile races that will determine which party controls the Senate for the next two years are extremely tight, according to a new CNN poll, as Maine and Kansas remain close and Democrats extended their leads in Texas and Michigan. Democrats, who are widely projected to win a majority in the House of Representatives, need to flip four Senate seats from red to blue in order to gain a 51-seat majority, protecting their majority from the vice presidential tiebreaker. Maine In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, is the only Republican incumbent running in a state that went for Kamala Harris in 2024. FOX NEWS POLL: NAIL-BITER IN MAINE SENATE RACE Collins' Democratic challenger is Troy Jackson, the former president of the state Senate who jumped into the race as a replacement for the previous nominee, scandal-plagued Graham Platner. The race has no clear frontrunner, according to the CNN poll, though Jackson holds a marginal lead. COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME' Forty-nine percent of respondents told the outlet's pollsters they favored Jackson, compared to 45% for Collins. While Jackson is slightly ahead, at least 12.5% of voters say they could still change their minds. Respondents tied Collins to her party less than any other Republican running for Senate in the nation, with 46% of respondents saying they believe she would choose her constituents over the Republican Party. DAVID MARCUS: THE FUTURE OF THE GOP IN NEW ENGLAND RIDES ON MAINE’S SENATE VOTE Collins was one of seven Republicans to vote in favor of President Donald Trump's second impeachment in 2021, and she joined Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, as the only Republicans to vote against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's Senate confirmation in 2025. With Collins managing to distance herself from Trump, her race has largely become a referendum on her own career. Three-quarters of respondents from either party told CNN pollsters that their choice was motivated more by Collins than Jackson. DAVID MARCUS: IN BLUE MAINE, NOBODY BELIEVES SUSAN COLLINS WILL LOSE UNTIL THEY SEE IT Michigan In Michigan, despite warnings from some mainstream Democrats and the state's Jewish community, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is building a lead over former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich. Respondents favored El-Sayed at 49% compared to the 42% who favored Rogers, according to the poll. CNN's previous poll, released in early September, showed El-Sayed with a 47% share compared to Rogers' 44%, showing the former public health director El-Sayed building on his lead. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS The Democrat has consolidated his party's support after a contentious primary with Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. Ninty-five percent of likely Democrat voters say they'll punch the ticket for El-Sayed, up from 90% in the September poll. Rogers voters, meanwhile, are motivated more by dislike for the Democratic candidate than faith in the Republican. 57% told CNN pollsters they were voting against El-Sayed, up from 41% in a previous poll. DAVID MARCUS: THE 5 FACTORS THAT COULD DECIDE MICHIGAN'S TIGHT AND UGLY SENATE RACE Rogers' favorability has also taken a hit, moving from 58% in September to 50% in October. Texas Texas State Rep. James Talarico also built upon a narrow lead over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, despite Talarico's extended absence from the campaign trail in early October. FOX NEWS POLL: TEXAS SENATE RACE GALLOPING TOWARD A PHOTO FINISH Forty-nine percent of likely voters told pollsters they'd vote for Talarico, while 43% said they would vote for Paxton, according to the poll. Texas, a state that has voted for exactly one new Democratic Senate candidate into office since Lyndon B. Johnson vacated his seat to become vice president, also voted more strongly for Trump in 2024 than in either of his previous elections. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK Despite the typically steadfast support for the GOP in the Lone Star State, Talarico is riding a wave of favorability and minority support to remain in pole position five days before polls close. CNN's poll says 64% of likely voters of color support Talarico, including 22% of the cohort that voted for Trump in 2024. Talarico is also leading Paxton in favorability within their own parties. 24% of Republicans have an unfavorable view of Paxton, according to the poll. Just 2% of Democrats, meanwhile, view Talarico unfavorably. Kansas In Kansas, a state which Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., is falling behind Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. Forty-nine percent of likely voters say they support Hamilton, 45% say they support Marshall. Hamilton, a relatively unknown candidate, is far outperforming his own party in a state where Democrats are broadly unfavorable. 57% of voters view the Democratic Party as unfavorable while only 38% of them feel the same about Hamilton. Like Republicans in Michigan, likely voters in Kansas appear to be more highly motivated by a dislike for one candidate than strong positive feelings for another. 59% of Hamilton backers say they're motivated by opposition to Marshall. Hamilton, a Christian pastor, is even drawing support from across the aisle. Roughly 12% of Republicans and Republican-leaning likely voters say they support Hamilton, according to the poll. Registered voters were randomly sampled, according to the outlet. 838 likely voters were considered in Kansas, 783 in Maine, 768 in Michigan and 923 in Texas. CNN tabulated its margins of sampling error at plus or minus 4.5% for Kansas and Maine, 4.7% in Michigan and 4.2% in Texas. Fox News Digital contacted all eight campaigns for further comment.

articles.title: Alaska governor orders investigation into Peltola camp after report they recruited second Dan Sullivan
articles.summary: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced Thursday that he is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after a report that it worked with allies to recruit a candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in an effort to dilute his votes.
articles.body: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced Thursday that he is ordering an investigation into Democrat Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after a report that it worked with allies to recruit a candidate with the same name as incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in an effort to dilute his votes. The Department of Public Safety would seek to determine “whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted,” Dunleavy said in an overnight post to X. “The evidence will determine what happens next.” Dunleavy, a Republican, referred to Wednesday’s revelations from a bombshell New York Times report as “disturbing new evidence” and said that “anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.” Also on Thursday, President Donald Trump cast doubt on whether Republicans would seat Peltola if she wins her race. Asked by a reporter whether he thought Republicans should refuse to seat Peltola if she wins, Trump said, “you’re going to have to see what happens.” He added it was “hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.” The Times published an explosive report detailing the campaign and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s alleged efforts to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as incumbent, citing interviews with 12 people who were involved with or were told about the plan, or were contacted as potential recruits. The report also cited dozens of text messages among participants. The Times’ report included information from Elisa Rios, Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired in August. Rios later contacted the Times and “retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race,” the outlet said. It also reported the she had been planning to file a wrongful termination lawsuit against the campaign but has not done so. The Times’ revelations have rocked the critical battleground race. Republicans have widely condemned Democrats for allegedly trying to manipulate the ballot in an attempt to confuse voters — an accusation the GOP has been making since the second Sullivan entered the race. NBC News previously reported that the second Sullivan’s candidacy was under investigation by state and federal prosecutors in Alaska, and a grand jury issued subpoenas for information from witnesses linked to his campaign in August. The Justice Department also filed a lawsuit last week seeking to block the certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan loses. NBC News has reached out to the Peltola campaign on Dunleavy’s announcement. Reached for comment on the governor’s post, a Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spokesperson provided a statement given to other news outlets. “The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” the spokesperson said, adding that Republicans “have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns.” Reached for comment Wednesday on the Times report, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said the campaign “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The campaign also pointed to instances of Republicans allegedly propping up “spoiler” candidates. NBC News has previously reported that people who worked to recruit challenger Sullivan did not necessarily violate the law. Stephen Richer, an election analyst for NBC News, said those involved in the recruitment could be in the clear legally if there was “no inducement, like money or threats” and the candidate ran “of his or her own volition, even if we don’t agree with the reasons that the person is choosing to run.” The Times did not report any evidence that Sullivan was coerced, and he has said he entered the race of his own accord. Following the report, Trump called for Peltola and the challenger Sullivan to be “removed from the ballot and prosecuted.” Asked by a reporter whether he agreed that Peltola should be prosecuted, Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday that “we should certainly look into whether she committed election fraud.” “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” he said later. “So whether it’s criminal or not, she certainly has committed, I think, a great moral failing, and hopefully the voters of Alaska punish her.” House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer, R-Ky., also said Thursday that his committee was requesting transcribed interviews with Rios and a Democratic operative, Jerid Kurtz, who reportedly was involved in recruiting the challenger Dan Sullivan. “If you do not voluntarily appear for the interview, we will be forced to evaluate the use of compulsory process,” Comer wrote in letters to the two. The Times reported that Kurtz did not respond to repeated requests for comment and made his social media accounts private. Both Democrats and Republicans have a history of trying to prop up candidates who could draw votes from their main opponents. But Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called the reported Peltola campaign effort “unprecedented” in an interview Thursday on Fox News, saying he believed the Sullivan saga “was a concerted effort to manipulate and to deceive the voters of Alaska.” “The voters of Alaska are going to see through that,” he said.

articles.title: NC’s redrawn 1st District is most expensive race in US
articles.summary: North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District has become the most expensive House race on record, according to new ad spending data shared this week. Democratic Rep. Don Davis (N.C.) is fighting for reelection in the newly redrawn district against GOP challenger Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel. A striking $52.9 million has been spent on the…
articles.body:
North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District has become the most expensive House race on record, according to new ad spending data shared this week.

Democratic Rep. Don Davis (N.C.) is fighting for reelection in the newly redrawn district against GOP challenger Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel.

A striking $52.9 million has been spent on the race so far, making it the most expensive House general election in the country’s history, according to AdImpact .

Nearly $30 million of this grand total has gone toward supporting the Democratic incumbent in the race, while the GOP nominee has received just more than $23 million in political ads.

Polling has indicated a tight match-up in the district, which was redrawn in a GOP-led effort to secure another seat for Republicans in the House. The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates the race as a “toss-up.”

In 2024, the 1st District House election reported a total of $38.5 million spent in the race, while less than $7 million was spent in the 2022 election, in which Davis was first elected.

Following North Carolina’s redistricting effort, Republicans saw the district as an opportunity for a pickup this midterm cycle as the GOP fights to maintain control over both chambers of Congress.

Democrats are aiming to retake power in the House, with Decision Desk HQ placing their odds at achieving this at around 80 percent as of Thursday. The fight for control of the Senate appears tighter, with Democrats having a 60 percent chance of gaining a majority in the upper chamber.

The 2026 midterms are shaping up to be one of the most expensive elections in history, with AdImpact projecting earlier this month that spending this cycle could soon exceed the $11.2 billion spent in the 2024 presidential election.

Eight of the 10 races included on the political ad spending tracker’s list of the most expensive House elections in history are from this year.

Two other tight House races in Florida’s 25th District and Michigan’s 7th District have also broken previous spending records, attracting a respective $49.4 million and $47.7 million in spending, according to AdImpact.

The 2024 House election in New York’s 19th Congressional District, which Democratic Rep. Josh Riley won, still ranks fourth on the list with a total of $47.2 million spent. Additionally, Maine’s 2024 race in the state’s 2nd District remains on AdImpact’s top 10 list.

A U.S. Attorney in Minnesota, appointed by then-President Joe Biden, eventually shut down the probe in 2021, a source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital. OMAR’S DELETED TWEET COULD GIVE CLUE ON ALLEGED MARRIAGE TO HER BROTHER Despite his own administration's investigation into Omar at the time she was running for the Minnesota House, Obama condemned the renewed probe, which included a Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raid on her Washington, D.C. home on Oct. 12. articles.title: 25 years later, 9/11 families are still fighting to get their day in court
articles.summary: Congress changed the law 10 years ago precisely to give the families a pathway to test their claims, which may or may not prevail in court.
articles.body:
The families of 9/11 victims have been fighting for more than two decades for the right to sue the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for its alleged role in the attacks. They may soon get their day in court — so long as a circuit court respects the will of Congress.

Not long after the attacks, which claimed nearly 3,000 lives , a troubling set of facts emerged. A majority of the hijackers were Saudi nationals . Although the Saudi government has denied involvement and the 9/11 Commission found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior officials individually funded al Qaeda, the country had been a major backer of charities that supported extremist ideologies. And some Saudi government officials had apparent connections to some of the attackers.

When victims’ families began suing the kingdom in 2002 , Saudi Arabia moved to have the claims dismissed based on the concept of sovereign immunity , which holds that a government may only be sued with its consent. Riyadh argued that a 1976 law — the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act — only allowed lawsuits to be filed against countries on the State Department’s list of terrorism sponsors.

In 2005, the federal district court agreed with Saudi Arabia, which wasn’t on the list. This prompted another decade of legal wrangling and uncertainty for the families. Finally, Congress intervened.

Overwhelming bipartisan majorities passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act in 2016 over President Obama’s veto . The 2016 law removed the requirement that a state sponsor of terror must be on the State Department’s list.

The 2016 law also made clear that a foreign government can be sued for monetary damages for “an act of international terrorism in the United States.” Critically, the injury must be caused by a wrongful act of the foreign government or “any official, employee, or agent of that foreign state,” while “acting within the scope” of his employment, even if the act occurred outside the U.S.

The 9/11 families have long argued that Fahad al-Thumairy and Omar al-Bayoumi — a Saudi diplomat and alleged intelligence asset, respectively — helped two of the hijackers in Southern California. The legal process resumed in 2017, and both men have become central to the legal dispute. Saudi Arabia, once again, sought to get the lawsuit dismissed on sovereign immunity grounds, but in August 2025, a district court ruled that the lawsuit could proceed.

The district court concluded that there was sufficient evidence to support, for jurisdictional purposes, a claim that al-Bayoumi met with two of the al Qaeda hijackers in 2000 and helped them open a bank account and find an apartment. It also held that al-Bayoumi and al-Thumairy coordinated “to some degree for the same goal.” The court emphasized that this was a preliminary finding to establish jurisdiction, and the families must still prove their claims at trial.

Saudi Arabia appealed to the Second Circuit, which heard oral arguments on Oct. 7. The lawyer representing Saudi Arabia told the court that “the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has never supported its enemy, al Qaeda, against its ally, the United States.”

He also argued that al-Bayoumi and al-Thumairy were not acting within the “scope of employment,” which the amended law requires before Saudi Arabia can be held responsible for their conduct. He argued that no one in the Saudi government directed them to assist the hijackers.

The appellate judges indicated that the issues are difficult and complex. Lawyers involved in the case reportedly do not expect a ruling until next year. Yet Congress changed the law 10 years ago precisely to give the families a pathway to test their claims, which may or may not prevail in court.

Whatever the outcome, families — and the nation more broadly — deserve the closure that a rigorous, fair and open legal process can bring.

Bryce Poole is a senior legal fellow in the Meese Institute for the Rule of Law at Advancing American Freedom

articles.body:
Republican strategist Karl Rove said Wednesday he expects President Trump will resume U.S. strikes against Iran after the midterm elections are over.

Rove made his prediction in an interview with Fox News’s Brian Kilmeade on his series “ The Brian Kilmeade Show ,” who asked the former adviser to former President George W. Bush if “we go back to kinetic action in Iran?”

“He has sort of signaled it,” Rove replied. “And if you look at what’s happening on the ground — two aircraft carriers in the region, a third one on the way, plus enough ground forces, plus enough air assets. If I were the Iranians, I’d be certainly thinking that’s what’s coming my way after the election.”

Trump has warned that the U.S. could attack Tehran after the midterms. The U.S. Central Command (Centcom) has plans ready to resume strikes if it receives authorization from the White House, a source aware of the plans previously told The Hill.

The $47 billion war against Iran has been at a standstill without a ceasefire or peace deal in place. Trump has touted the U.S.’s military prowess over Iran, claiming earlier this month at a campaign rally in Montana that Iran’s army is “decimated” and its “leaders are gone.”

“I should have probably left their leaders because I don’t know who the hell we’re negotiating with,” he quipped.

The president has also repeated his claim that the conflict will soon come to an end.

The U.S. military has more than 50,000 service members in the Middle East and about 20 warships, some of which are helping enforce the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea.

There are two aircraft carrier strike groups in the Middle East and a third one, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, is going to the Centcom region to possibly relieve the USS George Washington.

The eight-month conflict hit the world with an energy shortage after Iran effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported. Soaring gas prices grew to become a key issue in the midterm elections and could be one that voters punish Republican lawmakers over at the ballot box next week.

AAA estimated Thursday that the national average for gas in the U.S. costs $4.23, a $1.20 jump from the national average this time last year.

articles.summary: The Justice Department said Wednesday that agents and employees from the FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will not serve as poll monitors in the upcoming midterm elections. The department said in a court filing that employees from the Federal Bureau of Prisons, the Bureau ‌of ⁠Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the…
articles.body:
The Justice Department said Wednesday that agents and employees from the FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will not serve as poll monitors in the upcoming midterm elections.

The department said in a court filing that employees from the Federal Bureau of Prisons, the Bureau ‌of ⁠Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) will serve as poll monitors, but none from the FBI or ICE, according to a declaration filed Wednesday .

The filing comes after civil rights group NAACP filed a lawsuit to bar prosecutors and other law enforcement personnel from serving as election monitors.

According to the court filing, election monitors have been trained to not interfere in voting and to follow all rules of the assigned state or jurisdiction. Their primary role is to observe, ​take notes and interview willing voters outside polling places.

Additionally, the monitors will not be acting as law enforcement ​personnel while monitoring, and they are prohibited from carrying any firearms.

Earlier this year , the Department of Homeland Security said ICE officers would not be present in polling sites during the elections. In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE officers won’t go to patrol or monitor polling stations but can be present “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” The Guardian reported .

Citing Mullin’s remarks, the city of Denver filed a lawsuit to block ICE from going to voting sites. The filing argued that ordering federal officers to carry out detainments and serve warrants violated the “ troops at polls ” law, which imposes fines and potential jail time for federal officers being present at “any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

articles.title: Senators propose bipartisan changes in their chamber’s procedures
articles.summary: Sens. Jeff Merkley and Steve Daines proposed a four-part bipartisan agenda in a Washington Post op-ed aimed at reducing Senate dysfunction by reforming the filibuster and streamlining legislative processes.
articles.body:
It is often repeated, especially in the House, that the U.S. Senate has only two rules: unanimous consent and exhaustion.

Never mind that the Framers intentionally designed the upper chamber to slow things down. The apocryphal story is that when Thomas Jefferson returned to the U.S. from serving as ambassador to France, he asked George Washington, who had chaired the constitutional convention, “Why the Senate?” The general responded with a question: “Why do you pour your tea into that saucer.” “Why, to cool it,” replied Jefferson. “So too,” said Washington, “do we pour the hot legislation from the House into the cooling saucer of the Senate.”

Still, the convention did not intend for the Senate to be an inert body — an ant frozen in amber. It was purposely designed to take into account the interests of the various states, which originally appointed their senators, and not simply be a porous populist sieve.

Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Steve Daines (R-Mont.) recently proposed a bipartisan four-part agenda for limbering up the upper body. As they put it, “The Senate needs to be able to keep up to legislate effectively. So we have put together a plan to reward bipartisan cooperation, create more opportunities for senators to offer constructive amendments, and allow the chamber to bring more bills to the floor for public debate.”

Daines, a two-term senator who is retiring in January, would like his valedictory to be a positive contribution to making the Senate relevant again. Merkley, now in his third term, had previously served ten years in the Oregon state House of Representatives, where he rose to be Speaker. Like Daines, he is frustrated with the Senate just sitting around, “cooling it.”

Not surprisingly, at the heart of their plan is a proposal to dilute the controversial action-blocker known as the filibuster. The filibuster allows unlimited debate on the floor until three-fifths of senators vote to invoke cloture, to begin the procedure that ends the debate. Then, after 30 additional hours of talking, the pending measure comes to a final vote.

First, Merkley and Daines propose to “update” the cloture rule by eliminating the super-majority cloture requirement in certain instances, such as on routine procedural matters like the motion to proceed to consideration, and on amendments.

Secondly, they would eliminate the intervening day currently required between when a cloture motion is filed and when it is voted, and also eliminate the additional 30 hours of debate after cloture is invoked.

Third, they would create one day a week when legislation that has been “robustly” reported from a committee with the bipartisan support of at least a majority of each party, can be “fast-tracked” to floor consideration. The process would be initiated by a petition filed by the chair and ranking member of the committee, with the support of 16 senators for consideration of the measure, including specifying in the petition what amendments could be offered. Debate would be limited to six hours followed by final passage by majority vote of the Senate.

Fourth, Daines and Merkley would provide for a two-day fast-track consideration of bipartisan spending bills, allowing for just 20 relevant amendments equally divided between the parties. Again, these bills would be exempt from the 60-vote cloture requirement. This is not terribly radical, as this is already the case for 160 other categories of legislation such as budget resolutions, reconciliation bills, and joint resolutions repealing new federal regulations through the Congressional Review Act.

The Merkley-Daines agenda would enable the Senate to move on a more expedited and bipartisan basis, but it would not totally abolish of gridlock. Bipartisanship is hard to come by these days. So much depends not just on greater cooperation and consensus within committees, but also on party leaders being willing to compromise on what they are willing to give up. Partisan agendas and messaging will continue to dominate, especially in election years.

Some of the bipartisan proposals mimic House procedures already in place — for example, suspension of the rules, discharge petitions and privileged consideration of certain types of measures.

It reminds one of the musical lament in “My Fair Lady:” “ Why can’t a woman be more like a man? ” In this instance, the question is, “Why can’t the Senate be more like the House?” The resounding musical response from the American Founders’ chorus would be, “Because they are different, and you’re not going to change that!”

Ambassador Jefferson’s ghost might even concur: “Vive la difference!”

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran culminating as chief-of-staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial,” and “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

articles.title: Stephen A. Smith: Knicks players ‘don’t want to go’ to White House
articles.summary: Sports commentator Stephen A. Smith on Wednesday said the New York Knicks “don’t want to go” to the White House to celebrate their win at the 2026 NBA Finals. “This is what I’ve been hearing and I’m going to say it,” Smith said on ESPN’s “First Take.” “Don’t know how much truth there is to…
articles.body:
Sports commentator Stephen A. Smith on Wednesday said the New York Knicks “don’t want to go” to the White House to celebrate their win at the 2026 NBA Finals.

“This is what I’ve been hearing and I’m going to say it,” Smith said on ESPN’s “First Take.” “Don’t know how much truth there is to it because I haven’t heard from the players directly, but one of the things that people have been talking about around New York City, and around Madison Square Garden, is that the climate was a little bit different.”

“People have been a little bit stressed because the owner, James Dolan, has an attitude with players because they don’t want to go to the White House,” he added.

Smith said he does not “give a damn” about the situation and that he doesn’t know whether the story is true or not.

“But I believe anything when it comes to James Dolan, because he’s a walking embodiment of petulance,” he continued. “This man is as petty as they come.”

Smith said he was concerned that Dolan will tout the championship win, the team’s first in 53 years, and not win more beyond that.

“This guy, Dolan, I don’t trust him. … He is petty enough to have an attitude because he’s tight with Trump and wants to go to the White House,” he said in an animated plea for the team’s future. “And some of the players, if not most of them, might not want to go.”

The Hill has reached out to the Knicks media team for comment.

The Knicks defeated the San Antonio Spurs 94-90 in Game 5 of the championship series in June after facing a 16-point deficit. The victory ignited celebrations in the Big Apple, with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) saying he would award the team with keys to the city and hold a parade in their honor.

President Trump, invited by Dolan, attended Game 3 at Madison Square Garden, marking the first time that a sitting U.S. president attended an NBA Finals game in person. But fans at the game booed the president while he watched from Dolan’s private box during a rendition of the “Star Spangled Banner.”

No team that has won the NBA Finals has visited the White House during either of Trump’s terms, ESPN reported . The Boston Celtics were the first winning team to go to the White House, in 1963, when Brookline, Mass., native John F. Kennedy served as president. Champions visited the White House every year former President Obama was in office.

The Oklahoma City Thunder, which won in 2025, did not attend the White House last season because of timing issues.

articles.title: Trump DOJ's fight over 20K suspected noncitizen voters takes sharp turn as California ballots pour in
articles.summary: A federal judge blocked the Justice Department's bid to sequester ballots from over 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters on California's voter rolls.
articles.body: U.S. District Judge David O. Carter on Wednesday rejected the Justice Department's emergency request to force California to set aside mail-in ballots associated with more than 20,000 registered voters whose citizenship the Trump administration has questioned, ruling that the last-minute intervention would disrupt an election already underway. The over 20,000 voters identified by Department of Justice officials as "likely aliens" were designated as such after Homeland Security Investigations and federal partners "used multiple data-enrichment and verification methods" to flag potential noncitizens on California’s voter rolls. California officials, however, disputed the list's accuracy, citing a preliminary review that identified U.S.-born individuals and voters with no voting history among those flagged. Carter, a Clinton appointee, ruled that the Justice Department's last-minute effort to intervene in California's election violated constitutional and federal-law constraints, while questioning the reliability of the government's evidence that the flagged voters were noncitizens. "The district court denied our emergency request to sequester ballots from 20,000 suspected noncitizens," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution. The Solicitor General authorized an immediate appeal. We filed our Notice of Appeal and will immediately seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit." NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS The Trump administration has suffered a string of defeats in election-related cases in the lead-up to the midterm elections, raising questions whether the administration will be able to deliver on its promises of improved election integrity ahead of the 2028 presidential election. President Donald Trump and other administration officials have repeatedly raised concerns about widespread voter fraud in U.S. elections, though those claims have not been supported by evidence demonstrating fraud on such a broad scale. California election officials argued that complying with the Justice Department's request would be virtually impossible because county election offices had already processed more than 500,000 ballots, separating them from identifying information and preventing officials from reliably linking those votes to individual voters. Carter warned that the requested intervention would "wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway," though he noted that federal authorities were free to pursue individual voting fraud cases. Experts were divided along ideological lines in the case. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL Hans von Spakovsky, an election expert at Advancing American Freedom, a Mike Pence-affiliated think tank, criticized California for refusing to comply with the DOJ’s request. "It tells you something very revealing and unfortunately badly revealing about California officials that they don’t even want to check," von Spakovsky told The Center Square. "In California, for example, they have automatic voter registration. When you go in to get a driver’s license, they don’t ask you, ‘Would you also like to register to vote?’ The state of California just automatically registers you, and when you ask them, they say, ‘Well, it’s up to the individuals to tell us they’re not eligible to vote.’" BIDEN-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS VOTER-FRAUD PROBES IN BATTLEGROUND STATES JUST DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS Rick Hasen, a University of California, Los Angeles, election-law professor, meanwhile, called the Justice Department’s request a "total overreach of federal power," arguing that "the Constitution’s clear that states have the authority to run Congressional elections unless Congress passes a statute otherwise — and Congress didn’t do so here." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The California governor’s office did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

articles.title: Mammograms can reveal risk for heart disease
articles.summary: Health experts are calling for standardized reporting of breast arterial calcification on mammograms to improve cardiovascular disease prevention for women.
articles.body:
A 50-year-old woman goes in for her annual mammogram, and it comes back showing she is clear of cancer. But the scan also catches signs of calcium build up in her breast tissue arteries, a risk factor for future heart attack or stroke. The radiologist isn’t required to look at this measure, so it passes unnoticed.

The woman goes home relieved, unaware of the early warning about a disease with an even greater chance of killing her.

That marker is breast arterial calcification, or BAC . It’s already visible on the tens of millions of mammograms performed on women in the U.S. each year, with no extra cost or time needed to read it. Heart disease kills more American women than all cancers combined. Yet the radiologist who could spot BAC, the primary care doctor who could act on it, and the cardiologist who could treat it rarely confer.

Currently, no country mandates the reporting of BAC, and there are no established clinical pathways for follow up once it’s found. That gap is a missed opportunity to advance personalized risk stratification and early cardiovascular disease prevention that can keep women healthy as they age. Unfortunately, a woman’s care in midlife depends on where she lives, who she sees, or how her provider was trained, rather than a consistent, evidence-based standard.

We need to fix this broken system; establishing standards around reporting BAC and protocols providers can follow when BAC is detected can help advance an integrated approach to midlife health in women.

Some health systems have already had success in making BAC reporting operationally possible. Northwell Health has been reporting BAC across its 21 hospitals since 2024. Mount Sinai’s departments of radiology and cardiology work together to assess the prevalence of BAC and define best practices for reporting to patients.

The potential for impact is significant. A study at Stanford measured what happens when clinicians and patients are notified and shown coronaryartery calcification on a scan (a different but related kind of finding). Compared with usual care, patients and clinicians were more likely to take action: for example, researchers saw a meaningful increase in statin prescriptions as a result. The McKinsey Health Institute estimates that downstream preventative care based on risk identified by BAC would cost roughly $500 per woman and could prevent an estimated 17,000 – 60,000 cardiovascular events in the U.S. over seven years, avoiding billions in health care costs.

We don’t have to move political mountains to make BAC reporting on mammograms the norm. We can take a page from the breast cancer movement. Just three years ago, the FDA updated federal mammography regulations to require that providers notify women about the density of their breasts, since breast density can make cancer more difficult to detect on a mammogram. This was achieved through sustained coordination among patient advocates — most notably the late Dr. Nancy Cappello and JoAnn Pushkin — and organizations like Susan G. Komen, state lawmakers, bipartisan congressional champions such as Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) and the late-Sen. Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), and the FDA.

In the same way key stakeholders came together to standardize breast density reporting, there are critical actors who have the power to make BAC reporting the norm.

Radiologists and their professional societies need to set standards around BAC reporting so there is more consistency in how BAC is graded. This will go a long way toward ensuring more women have access to actionable information that, together with their care team, they can use to inform their preventative healthcare.

The FDA should require BAC reporting, just as it now requires breast density reporting. But, importantly, states don’t need to wait for the federal government to act. They can follow the lead of Maryland, which just last Thursday became the first state to mandate BAC reporting on mammograms. Maryland achieved this by adding language on BAC to the law on breast density notification that most states have on the books, rather than writing new legislation from scratch.

That said, health systems should indeed build clinical protocols, as Mount Sinai and Northwell already do, so that when BAC is discovered on a patient’s mammogram, the radiologist can work with her care team to develop pathways that lead to a more complete cardiovascular risk assessment. The Institute Advancing Women’s Health and the Washington Research Foundation are co-funding research to accelerate the implementation of BAC diagnosis and reporting in diverse health systems.

None of this requires new science. Women often navigate fragmented care systems where symptoms affecting the heart, brain, bones, metabolism, mood, sleep, and reproductive health are treated separately rather than as part of a broader health transition. Standardizing protocols for BAC is a concrete place to start closing that gap and supporting women in midlife. We have all of the tools in place to make change happen — now we need the will to act.

Paula Schneider, former CEO of Susan G. Komen, currently serves as CEO of the Institute Advancing Women’s Health (InAWH), a new, global nonprofit focused on closing the gap between what is known and what is done in women’s midlife health care. Erica Spatz, M.D., MHS, is Associate Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine and Associate Professor of Epidemiology (Chronic Diseases) at Yale School of Medicine and a member of InAWH’s Medical Advisory Board.

Republicans call for Peltola investigation

Programming note : We’re Claire Leibowitz and Abigail Walker, filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to cleibowitz@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com .

Mark Thiessen, Alex Brandon & Becky Bohrer; Associated Press

Backlash against Senate hopeful former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) is growing, with the president and GOP lawmakers demanding an investigation into allegations that she plotted with Senate Democrats to insert a spoiler candidate into the race.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) on Wednesday night called for an investigation into Peltola and her campaign, pointing to reporting from The New York Times which found that Democrats secretly recruited a candidate with same name as Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) to boost their chances.

Peltola’s campaign denies the accusations .

“This is voter fraud at the highest level,” Trump said while rallying in Ohio Wednesday night. He later added, referring to Democrats, “That’s what they’re good at – cheating.”

“There’s no doubt that Mary Peltola has been, at least her campaign and the Democrat apparatus, they are involved in collusion,” Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) told NewsNation’s Katie Pavlich on Wednesday. “They’ve been colluding together in a coordinated effort to deceive the voters.”

Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), who had criticized the Department of Justice for its pre-emptive lawsuit over the double name, also joined in and called for “truth.”

“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” the senator wrote in a statement to The Hill. “Run and win on your merits: your views, your policy ideas, and your accomplishments.”

Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) announced she’d remain in support of Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed , despite her fiancé’s public decision to vote for former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

“Like a lot of households in America, we’re a household divided,” Stevens told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins. “I still very much want our Democratic nominee, his name is Abdul, to win this race.”

El-Sayed narrowly beat Stevens in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary in August. Shortly after, Stevens put her support behind the progressive candidate.

Diverging opinions : In an interview published Wednesday, Stevens’s fiancé Jason Turkish said he’d back Rogers and cited what he felt was antisemitic language from El-Sayed’s campaign as his reasoning.

“We have never seen a candidate for U.S. Senate act so recklessly toward the safety of Jews in the community as we have seen from Abdul,” Turkish told The Detroit News.

“Every time he talks about genocide, Jews get death threats,” he added, referring to conversations about Israel’s ongoing war in Gaza.

There are only five more days until Election Day, and candidates are working to leave their final mark on voters.

President Trump is continuing is GOP campaign crusade on Thursday, returning to South Carolina for Sen. Darline Graham. He is expected to give remarks in Rock Hill at 12:30 p.m. EDT.

Recent polls show Graham, the sister of late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), neck and neck with Democrat opponent Annie Andrews.

Vance heads to Texas, too: Vice President Vance is heading to Weatherford, Texas, to bolster support for the state’s attorney general Ken Paxton. He’s also facing a tighter-than-expected race with Democrat James Talarico.

Trump visited Texas three times in October. His most recent visit on Tuesday was met with a dueling rally hosted by Talarico in Lubbock.

Vance’s remarks are expected at 1:50 p.m. EDT.

And, in the Peach State: Former Vice President Harris is stumping for Sen. Jon Ossoff in his reelection bid. Former President Obama visited the state Wednesday night to talk affordability — and the Cheesecake Factory.

“First of all, let me get this on the record. I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory? I lived at Chuck E. Cheese and California Pizza Kitchen and the Cheesecake Factory. That was my jam for about a decade,” Obama said.

“Of course, the real problem is the price has gotten so high, a lot of folks can barely afford to go out to eat, so you would think that this administration would be spending time worrying about that,” he added.

Ossoff is favored to beat Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.).

Harris will speak in Macon, Ga., at 1:45 p.m. EDT.

The White House is getting an early start on Halloween tonight, courtesy of Trump and first lady Melania Trump.

Thousands of children and parents will get to trick-or-treat around the South Lawn. The U.S. Air Force Strolling Strings will play “traditional Halloween songs,” per a White House press release.

There are many festivities planned from many administration groups: The U.S. Postal Service will provide toy mail trucks and a post card station. The U.S. Department of Agriculture will host a giant pumpkin photo opp and hand out mini pumpkins from American farmers. The Treasury Department will share coloring books as a promotion for Trump Accounts.

Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, who was the director for strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff J5, was removed from his role this week because of “severe misconduct,” according to U.S. officials aware of the decision.

“The Department of War has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information. Anyone who compromises sensitive national security information puts the lives of our Warriors at risk and undermines every military operation that keeps our country safe,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on the social platform X .

Hegseth has fired more than two dozen high-level officials, drawing criticism from both Democrats and Republicans. Many of the cases have been unrelated to any disciplinary actions.

“Elon Musk is a genius, he’s just a real genius,” Putin said at a summit in Moscow, per Russia’s state media organization TASS.

The Russian president added the Kremlin was in conversations with Musk about developing a rival satellite communications system to SpaceX’s Starlink, which Ukraine currently uses in its military operations.

Starlink’s military-grade counterpart, Starshield, has been the subject of controversy in recent weeks when its capabilities were slowed in Ukraine , drawing backlash from both GOP and Democratic lawmakers.

Both Trump and Musk denied responsibility throughout the conflict, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has since stated that the technology has returned to typical function.
